The log link turns each coefficient into a **rating relativity**: $e^{\beta_j}$ is the multiplicative effect on frequency of a one-unit increase in $x_j$, which is exactly how rating algorithms are built
With log links on both, relativities multiply and coefficients add.

requirements.statement: A holdout sample is a portion of the data withheld from model fitting and used afterward to test or validate the model's predictive power on data it was not fitted to.

places.quote: A **Holdout Sample** is data deliberately kept out of model building so the finished model can be tested on observations it has never seen.

requirements.statement: Choose the holdout sample so that it is representative of the fitting data, for example by using alternating (even/odd) years rather than a block of the latest years, so that trends or changes in risk profile over time appear in both the holdout and fitting samples.

places.quote: Relativities fitted on the even years, and observed in the odd years (the holdout), are:

requirements.statement: The sum of squared prediction errors (SSE) between each method's predictions and the holdout sample's observed values measures predictive accuracy for that method.

places.quote: $$\text{SSE}_{\text{hold}} = \sum_{j} w_j \left(\hat{R}_j - R_j^{\text{hold}}\right)^2$$

requirements.statement: The prediction method with the lowest holdout SSE is the best predictor; a credibility procedure that beats the hazard group mean and raw data in SSE improves predictions, while one with higher SSE than a competitor for a class does not improve it there.

places.quote: A finer set of classes is only worth having if it predicts the holdout better than a coarser one.

requirements.statement: Shifting risk parameters over time reduce the correlation between years' experience as the lag between years increases, so a declining correlation by lag indicates shifting parameters.

places.quote: Mahler showed that risk parameters shift over time, so older years predict less.

requirements.statement: A chi-squared test of whether parameters shift over time computes the sum of (O-E)^2/E, compares it to a critical value, and rejects the null hypothesis of no shift if the statistic exceeds the critical value.

requirements.statement: A two-dimensional (occurrence/aggregate) ILF table is consistent if its factors satisfy the marginal-consistency conditions along both the occurrence-limit and aggregate-limit dimensions.
requirements.concept: Two-Dimensional Consistency Test for Increased Limits Factors

requirements.statement: Holding the aggregate limit fixed, ILFs must increase with the occurrence limit at a decreasing rate: the marginal rate per dollar of additional occurrence limit must not increase as the occurrence limit rises.
requirements.concept: Marginal Consistency of Increased Limits Factors

places.quote: So the *marginal* indemnity cost per dollar of additional limit must not increase as the limit rises; an indemnity ILF table whose marginal cost increases is not consistent with any size-of-loss distribution.

requirements.statement: Holding the occurrence limit fixed, ILFs must increase with the aggregate limit at a decreasing marginal rate per dollar of additional aggregate limit.
requirements.concept: Marginal Consistency of Increased Limits Factors

places.quote: So the *marginal* indemnity cost per dollar of additional limit must not increase as the limit rises; an indemnity ILF table whose marginal cost increases is not consistent with any size-of-loss distribution.

requirements.statement: Marginal consistency test: compute the slope (difference in ILF divided by difference in limit) between adjacent limits on each side of the missing factor, and require the slope below to be at least the slope above; this gives bounds on the unknown ILF from neighboring cells.
requirements.concept: Marginal Consistency of Increased Limits Factors

requirements.statement: Factor comparison test: the increase in ILF from raising the aggregate (or occurrence) limit must be larger at a lower fixed level of the other limit than at a higher level, so the difference between columns/rows is compared across adjacent limits to bound the unknown.

requirements.concept: Two-Dimensional Consistency Test for Increased Limits Factors

requirements.statement: A risk-loaded increased limit factor (ILF) is the ratio of the risk-loaded premium (expected loss plus risk load) at the policy limit to the risk-loaded premium at the basic limit.

places.quote: Palmer's fuller formulation puts it inside the factor: $\text{ILF}(L) = \dfrac{\text{LAS}(L) + \text{ALAE}(L) + \text{ULAE}(L) + \text{RL}(L)}{\text{LAS}(B) + \text{ALAE}(B) + \text{ULAE}(B) + \text{RL}(B)}$
Expected loss plus the risk load is the **risk-loaded technical premium**: the price a pricing model indicates for the risk itself, before expenses and commercial adjustments.

requirements.statement: With a standard-deviation risk load, the premium at a limit is E[X;L] + k·σ(X;L), where k is the selected percentage and σ is the standard deviation of the loss capped at that limit (no expenses assumed).

places.quote: *standard deviation*: $P = E[X] + k\,\sigma(X)$ — the load scales with share, so a 50% share pays half;
the standard deviation principle $E[X] + k\,\sigma(X)$ and the variance principle $E[X] + k\,\text{Var}(X)$ — measure volatility around the mean rather than the tail

requirements.statement: To get the loss distribution at a policy limit, cap each loss at the limit (g(x;L) = min(x, L)) and keep the original probabilities; losses above the limit become the limit.

places.quote: Also written $E[\min(X, u)]$; the **limited loss variable** is $Y = \min(X, u)$
Under a limit $u$ and no other modification, the insurer pays the whole loss $X$ when it is below $u$ and pays $u$ when it is not, so the payment is the limited loss variable $X \wedge u$

requirements.statement: The limited expected value is E[min(X,L)] = Σ p_i·min(x_i, L) for a discrete distribution, and the second moment is E[min(X,L)²] = Σ p_i·min(x_i, L)².

**Expected Value** ($E[X]$, also called the mean $\mu$) is the probability-weighted average of all values a [[Random Variable]] $X$ can take

requirements.statement: For losses uniformly distributed on [0, M], the mean is M/2 and the excess ratio at L is ((M−L)/M)^2.

The experience modification is Mod = Z × (AER − EER) / EER, where AER is the actual experience ratio, EER the expected experience ratio, and Z the credibility.

requirements.statement: Actual experience ratio AER = (includable limited losses + additional reported unreported loss liability (ARULL)) / company subject loss cost.

places.quote: $A$ is the insured's actual losses over the experience period and $E$ the losses expected for a risk of its size and class.
Put both at the same maturity, or complete the actual losses with the expected unreported:

requirements.statement: Additional unreported loss layer (ARULL) for each policy year and coverage = company subject loss cost × expected experience ratio × loss development factor.

the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method]] uses the *complement* $(1 - 1/\text{CDF})$ to weight an a priori expectation.

requirements.statement: Determine credibility, expected experience ratio, and maximum single loss by finding the bracket of the table containing the total company subject loss cost (summed over the experience period).

For a claims-made policy, the first-year (latest) claims-made policy period has an LDF of zero (no development applied) because claims-made losses are reported within the period; only occurrence years in the experience period use the development factors in ARULL.

requirements.statement: Includable losses in the experience period are limited to the maximum single loss (MSL), and the experience period consists of the prior policy years excluding the most recent year, summed across years.
requirements.concept: Includable Losses and Maximum Single Loss

places.quote: Experience rating is **prospective**: it uses a completed experience period (typically three years, excluding the most recent, incomplete one) to modify the *coming* policy's premium.

**In experience rating (Exam 8)** the risk's own experience $A$ is usually three completed policy years, excluding the most recent immature one. It is capped per claim, or split into primary and excess.

requirements.statement: In an experience rating plan with credibility Z, the experience modification is M = Z*(A − E)/E + 1, equivalently M = (A + K)/(E + K) when Z = E/(E + K), where A is actual loss, E is expected loss and K is a constant.

places.quote: $$M = Z \times \frac{A}{E} + (1 - Z)$$
$$M = Z\,\frac{A}{E} + (1 - Z) = \frac{A + K}{E + K}$$

requirements.statement: Standard premium is the manual premium multiplied by the experience mod, and the standard loss ratio is losses divided by standard premium.

places.quote: Order of application: schedule and experience modifications apply to the manual premium to give **standard premium**, which is then the base for a retro plan or a large-deductible programme.
$$\text{Standard Premium} = \text{Manual Premium} \times M$$
The standard loss ratio is the manual loss ratio divided by the mod:

places.quote: Rank risks by mod and form five groups.

requirements.statement: An effective plan yields roughly equal standard loss ratios across mod groups; standard loss ratios that rise with the mod indicate the plan gives too little credibility to actual experience and under-corrects the differences it identifies.

places.quote: Standard loss ratios falling as the mod rises mean too much credibility; rising means too little.

requirements.statement: Manual loss ratios that rise with the mod show that the plan successfully identifies differences in risk quality.

places.quote: The *manual* loss ratio should rise with the mod, showing the plan *identifies* differences.

places.quote: The **efficiency test** compares $\mathrm{Var}(\text{standard LR}) / \mathrm{Var}(\text{manual LR})$ across plans, and the lower value is better.

requirements.statement: Workers compensation losses are highly skewed, so a linear credibility estimate differs from the optimal estimate; splitting losses into primary and excess components reduces skewness and improves predictive accuracy.

A constant K implies loss ratio variance falls with risk size, which is not necessarily true; letting K increase with risk size keeps credibility of large risks below 1 and avoids large risks being essentially self-rated.

A quintile (or decile) test sorts data into groups by predicted relativity and compares each group's predicted values with the actual holdout values, with the data split into a test (training) set and a holdout set.

places.quote: A **Holdout Sample** is data deliberately kept out of model building so the finished model can be tested on observations it has never seen.

A **quantile plot** (or lift chart by predicted quantile) sorts a held-out dataset by predicted loss cost, splits it into equal-exposure buckets, and plots the actual against the predicted average in each.

requirements.statement: To judge whether credibility is overstated or understated, compute the ratio of predicted to actual (holdout) relativity by quintile and look for a pattern; with correctly calibrated credibility there should be no pattern.

places.quote: $$\text{Error}_q = \frac{\text{Predicted}_q}{\text{Actual}_q} - 1$$
Three criteria pick the winning model: **predictive accuracy** — does each bucket's actual match its predicted level?

Overstated credibility makes predictions too extreme (like the raw data), while understated credibility makes predictions stay too close to the countrywide average, so the credibility-weighted prediction should be compared with the holdout, not with the raw test data.
The sum of squared errors (SSE) in a quintile test is the sum over quintiles of the squared difference between predicted and holdout relativity; a lower SSE indicates a better-fitting predictor.

places.quote: The **Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)** (also called the **Sum of Squared Errors, SSE**) measures the total unexplained variability in a regression model — the sum of squared differences between observed and fitted values.
$$\text{MSE}_{\text{val}} = \frac{1}{n_v}\sum_{i \in \text{val}}\left(y_i - \hat{f}(x_i)\right)^2$$

requirements.statement: A credibility procedure is validated by having lower SSE than the alternatives (such as the complement/countrywide average and the raw data), so the method with the lowest SSE should be used.

places.quote: Cross-validation is what turns the [[Bias-Variance Tradeoff]] into a decision: training error falls monotonically with complexity, while CV error is U-shaped, and its minimum marks the right model size
B wins on training error but loses on the hold-out: it is overfitting, so choose A.

requirements.statement: The goals of an experience rating plan include safety incentive (the plan should reward insureds for controlling losses and so encourage loss prevention) and predictive accuracy (the experience mod should accurately predict the insured's future losses).

places.quote: It creates a real incentive for loss control, and an equally real incentive for **claim suppression** — paying small claims outside the policy to keep them out of the mod.
A mod is a prospective estimate of loss potential, not a charge-back for past losses.

In the NCCI experience rating plan, each loss is split at a split point into a primary layer (losses below the split point, which mainly reflect frequency) and an excess layer (losses above it, which reflect severity), and each layer receives its own credibility weight.
requirements.concept: NCCI Experience Rating Plan Primary/Excess Split

places.quote: the split between primary (capped) and excess losses is the mechanism the NCCI workers compensation formula uses to weight frequency more heavily than severity — the theory being that frequency is more predictive of future experience than severity.
Each loss is split at a split point, \$18,000 in most states, into a primary part that reflects frequency and an excess part that reflects severity.

requirements.statement: Giving zero credibility to excess losses removes the severity information from the mod, which lowers predictive accuracy, and removes the insured's incentive to control large losses, which lowers safety incentive.
requirements.concept: NCCI Experience Rating Plan Primary/Excess Split

places.quote: the split between primary (capped) and excess losses is the mechanism the NCCI workers compensation formula uses to weight frequency more heavily than severity — the theory being that frequency is more predictive of future experience than severity.
Each loss is split at a split point, \$18,000 in most states, into a primary part that reflects frequency and an excess part that reflects severity.

requirements.statement: If the split point is not indexed, inflation pushes more of each loss into the primary layer cap and more claims above the split point, so the expected loss ratios and D-ratios become outdated and mismatched with actual losses, lowering predictive accuracy.
requirements.concept: NCCI Experience Rating Plan Primary/Excess Split

places.quote: A fixed retention **leverages [[Inflation|inflation]]** into the excess layer.
Ideally the procedure censors *trended* losses, or indexes the threshold, since layers above a fixed threshold inflate faster.

requirements.statement: An insured with high claim frequency but no large losses has mostly primary losses, so putting more weight on primary or small losses, or none on excess losses, raises its mod.

places.quote: **A has a frequency problem** — forty claims where the class expects far fewer — which is persistent, controllable and highly predictive of next year.
Both had \$60,000 of losses, but B's frequency earns a debit mod and A's single large claim a credit, which is how the plan treats frequency as the better predictor.

requirements.statement: The NCCI experience rating modification is M = (Ap + W·Ae + (1−W)·Ee + B)/(E + B), where Ap is actual primary losses, Ae actual excess losses, Ee expected excess losses, E expected losses, W the excess-loss weight, and B (balance point) and K (credibility-related constant) vary with risk size.

Constant B and K rest on the law of large numbers: the variance of a risk's loss ratio falls in inverse proportion to risk size, so large risks are more stable and receive greater credibility, approaching full self-rating.
requirements.concept: Experience Rating Credibility and Risk Size

places.quote: - Credibility rises with size. A small risk's mod stays near $1.0$ however good or bad its recent record, because a few claims say little; a large risk approaches $Z = 1$ and effectively self-rates.

It requires the $X_i$ to be i.i.d. with finite mean $\mu$; the standard proof also assumes finite variance $\sigma^2$ and applies Chebyshev's inequality to $\bar{X}_n$, which has $\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \sigma^2/n$.

requirements.statement: Empirical NCCI studies show that loss ratio variance does not decline as fast with risk size as the law of large numbers predicts, because some sources of variation (changing conditions, parameter risk, long-tailed losses, heterogeneous operations in large risks) do not diminish with size; hence B and K should increase with size and no risk should be fully self-rated.
requirements.concept: Experience Rating Credibility and Risk Size

requirements.statement: The quintile test compares experience rating plans by sorting risks (within size groups) by mod into five groups, computing standard (modified) loss ratios and manual loss ratios for each quintile, and comparing the variance of standard loss ratios relative to manual loss ratios; the plan with the lower ratio performs better.

places.quote: Rank risks by mod and form five groups. The *manual* loss ratio should rise with the mod, showing the plan *identifies* differences. The *standard* (modified) loss ratio should be flat, showing the plan *corrects* for them.

requirements.statement: The efficiency test compares plans without grouping by mod, using the ratio of variance of modified (standard premium) loss ratios to variance of manual premium loss ratios as a test statistic, with a smaller statistic indicating a better plan.

places.quote: The **efficiency test** compares $\mathrm{Var}(\text{standard LR}) / \mathrm{Var}(\text{manual LR})$ across plans, and the lower value is better.
