places.quote: Offsets are also used to carry forward previously-determined relativities (e.g., an established deductible or territory relativity) into a new model without re-estimating them
Their factors belong outside the fitted model, set by loss elimination and entered as offsets, so that selection effects do not leak into them.

territory is modelled outside the GLM by other techniques, such as spatial smoothing. The GLM still has to account for it, so each policy record is populated with its indicated territory loss cost from the standalone model, entered as an offset.

requirements.statement: A risk-adjusted increased limit factor incorporates a risk load that grows with the policy limit (e.g., based on variance or standard deviation of losses, using a constant k) into the limited-limit expected loss, so the load is embedded in the ILF.

places.quote: *standard deviation*: $P = E[X] + k\,\sigma(X)$ — the load scales with share, so a 50% share pays half;

Palmer's fuller formulation puts it inside the factor: $\text{ILF}(L) = \dfrac{\text{LAS}(L) + \text{ALAE}(L) + \text{ULAE}(L) + \text{RL}(L)}{\text{LAS}(B) + \text{ALAE}(B) + \text{ULAE}(B) + \text{RL}(B)}$, where the **risk load** covers process and parameter risk, both of which vary by limit.

requirements.statement: The standard ILF derivation assumes that expenses and the profit and contingency provision are a constant percentage of premium (variable) and the same across all limits, so varying profit and contingency by limit with non-risk-adjusted ILFs departs from that assumption.

places.quote: Werner's indicated ILF is the ratio of losses and LAE at the two limits, assuming all underwriting expenses are variable and the variable expense and profit provisions do not vary by limit.

requirements.statement: Premium equals (pure premium plus fixed expense) divided by (1 minus variable expense and profit/contingency provision); fixed expenses should not vary by limit, while variable expense and profit loads are percentages of premium.

places.quote: $$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

$$\text{Indicated Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.concept: Risk Load Calculation for Increased Limit Factors

requirements.statement: A risk-adjusted ILF is mathematically grounded but its load is embedded in the pure premium and less visible to laypersons, whereas an explicit profit and contingency load by limit is more transparent and easily understood by non-technical audiences.

The efficiency test statistic (Fisher et al.) is the ratio of the variance of the standard (modified) loss ratios across quintiles to the variance of the manual loss ratios across quintiles; a smaller ratio means a more equitable plan.

places.quote: The **efficiency test** compares $\mathrm{Var}(\text{standard LR}) / \mathrm{Var}(\text{manual LR})$ across plans, and the lower value is better.

requirements.statement: To perform the efficiency test, sort risks by experience mod (or by manual loss ratio), group them into quintiles with equal numbers of risks, and sum manual premium, standard premium and loss within each quintile to compute quintile manual and standard loss ratios.

places.quote: Rank risks by mod and form five groups.

places.quote: $$\text{Modified Premium} = \text{Manual Premium} \times M$$
The standard loss ratio is the manual loss ratio divided by the mod:

places.quote: Standard loss ratios falling as the mod rises mean too much credibility; rising means too little.

requirements.statement: Standard loss ratios that fall across quintiles indicate the plan gives too much credibility to experience (high-mod risks overcharged, low-mod risks undercharged).

places.quote: Standard loss ratios falling as the mod rises mean too much credibility; rising means too little.

requirements.statement: In a competitive market, an insurer whose experience rating plan misprices a group of risks suffers adverse selection: the overpriced risks leave for competitors and the underpriced risks stay or join, eroding the insurer's loss ratio and profitability, whereas an insurer with an equitable plan (efficiency statistic near zero) faces little adverse selection.

places.quote: **Adverse Selection** is the tendency for those who know they are worse-than-average risks to buy more insurance, and better-than-average risks to buy less, when the insurer cannot distinguish between them.
A competitor with the better plan would take the Q1 business and leave Q5 behind.

requirements.statement: The multi-dimensional credibility estimate for a quantity is the complement of credibility (storm zone/overall) mean for that quantity plus the sum over each type of its coefficient times (sector mean minus zone mean) for that type, including the type being estimated.
The single-dimensional credibility estimate equals Z times the sector's observed mean plus (1 - Z) times the complement (storm zone) mean.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \cdot \bar{X} + (1-Z) \cdot \mu$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$

requirements.statement: Multi-dimensional credibility assumes the frequencies of different types (e.g. storm types) are positively correlated, so experience in other types in the sector informs the estimate for the target type, whereas single-dimensional credibility uses only the target type's own experience.

places.quote: Couret and Venter estimate each WC class's vector of claim frequencies by injury type with multi-dimensional credibility, so each injury type's estimate draws on the class's other injury counts.

requirements.statement: In multi-dimensional credibility, a sector whose other-type frequencies exceed the zone's raises the estimate above the complement mean (positive coefficient times positive deviation), which can outweigh a negative deviation in the target type and make the estimate higher than the single-dimensional one.

A quintile (decile) plot of experience rating performance groups risks by their experience mod and compares loss ratios across the groups; the standard loss ratio is loss divided by standard premium (manual premium times the mod), so standard LR = manual LR / mod.

places.quote: Rank risks by mod and form five groups. The *manual* loss ratio should rise with the mod, showing the plan *identifies* differences. The *standard* (modified) loss ratio should be flat, showing the plan *corrects* for them.

requirements.statement: A well-performing experience rating plan produces standard loss ratios that are roughly flat across mod quintiles, because the mod then fully corrects for differences in risk quality.

places.quote: The *standard* (modified) loss ratio should be flat, showing the plan *corrects* for them.

requirements.statement: To evaluate a plan with no current experience rating, compare the standard loss ratios (with the mod) to the implied manual loss ratios (without the mod, i.e. SLR times mod); if the standard LR is flatter/less dispersed than the manual LR, the mod is correcting for risk differences and should be implemented.

places.quote: Rank risks by mod and form five groups. The *manual* loss ratio should rise with the mod, showing the plan *identifies* differences. The *standard* (modified) loss ratio should be flat, showing the plan *corrects* for them.

requirements.statement: Experience rating improves premium equity and reduces adverse selection, since without it worse-than-average risks are underpriced and better risks overpriced.

places.quote: It improves equity, strengthens the incentive for loss control, and makes more risks acceptable to write.

places.quote: Standard loss ratios falling as the mod rises mean too much credibility; rising means too little.

requirements.statement: The efficiency test statistic measures the remaining unexplained variation in standard loss ratios across quintiles, so a lower value indicates a better-performing plan.

places.quote: The **efficiency test** compares $\mathrm{Var}(\text{standard LR}) / \mathrm{Var}(\text{manual LR})$ across plans, and the lower value is better.

requirements.statement: To decide between a current and proposed experience rating plan, compare their quintile standard loss ratio charts for flatness and their efficiency test statistics, and keep the plan that is flatter and has the lower statistic (when implementation cost is negligible).

places.quote: The **efficiency test** compares $\mathrm{Var}(\text{standard LR}) / \mathrm{Var}(\text{manual LR})$ across plans, and the lower value is better.

requirements.statement: The experience rating modification is Mod = Z*(A/E) + (1-Z), equivalently 1 + Z*(A-E)/E, where A is actual experience-period losses, E is expected losses, and Z is the credibility.

places.quote: The standard loss ratio is the manual loss ratio divided by the mod:

requirements.statement: An effective experience rating plan makes standard loss ratios more homogeneous across risks than manual loss ratios, so a standard loss ratio far from the others signals the mod over- or under-reacted (e.g., too much weight on actual experience).

places.quote: The *standard* (modified) loss ratio should be flat, showing the plan *corrects* for them. Standard loss ratios falling as the mod rises mean too much credibility; rising means too little.

requirements.statement: Plan improvements include capping (limiting) individual claim losses so large claims do not unduly affect the mod, or reducing the credibility given to actual experience.

It is capped per claim, or split into primary and excess.

places.quote: The **efficiency test** compares $\mathrm{Var}(\text{standard LR}) / \mathrm{Var}(\text{manual LR})$ across plans, and the lower value is better.

requirements.statement: To show a plan change improves the plan, recompute the mod and standard loss ratio under the changed plan (e.g., with capped losses or new credibility), then compare the efficiency statistic before and after the change.

\text{BP} = e - (\text{LCF} - 1)\,E + \text{LCF} \times I

places.quote: The **Table M charge** $\phi(r) = \mathrm{E}[\max(A/E - r,\,0)]$ is the expected loss above $rE$ per unit of $E$

requirements.statement: A guaranteed cost policy has a fixed premium known at inception, giving stable cash flow, but it does not adjust for good loss experience and typically costs more upfront because the insurer bears all loss variability.

A large dollar deductible policy has the insured reimburse losses within the deductible per occurrence, which lowers premium (and premium taxes) but makes the insured's cash flow less certain, depending on claim count and severity.

places.quote: *Large deductible:* the insurer pays every claim and bills the deductible back. It must have a per-occurrence limit, may have an aggregate, and has no minimum. Reimbursements are not premium, so they escape premium tax.

in this model, variable expense and profit are no longer loaded on the retained layer, which outweighs the processing, credit and risk charges, and the insured keeps the cash for its retained losses until they are paid.

requirements.statement: A retrospectively rated policy adjusts the final premium to actual losses subject to minimum and maximum limits (aggregate cap), rewarding good loss experience and safety efforts but making premium fluctuate as losses develop.

places.quote: **Retrospective Rating** adjusts a policy's premium *after* the period, based on the insured's own losses during that period, within a guaranteed minimum and maximum.

requirements.statement: To build a loss ratio plot, sort observations by the model's predicted value (e.g., predicted loss cost) in ascending order, group them, and plot actual loss ratio (actual loss divided by earned premium) for each group.

places.quote: The **loss ratio chart**: sort on predicted loss cost divided by current premium. A flat actual loss ratio means the plan already prices every segment; a rising one measures its inequity.

requirements.statement: A loss ratio plot assesses lift, i.e., how well a model differentiates good and bad risks (an upward trend in actual loss ratio across sorted predictions indicates lift); models giving the same sort order yield identical loss ratio plots.

places.quote: The **loss ratio chart**: sort on predicted loss cost divided by current premium. A flat actual loss ratio means the plan already prices every segment; a rising one measures its inequity.

requirements.statement: A simple quintile plot sorts observations by model-predicted value into five groups of roughly equal exposure and plots the average predicted and actual values for each group; a model is better when predicted and actual lines are closer and monotonic.

places.quote: A **quantile plot** (or lift chart by predicted quantile) sorts a held-out dataset by predicted loss cost, splits it into equal-exposure buckets, and plots the actual against the predicted average in each.

A [[Quantile Plot|quantile plot]] sorts records by predicted loss cost into equal-exposure buckets and compares actual with predicted in each, judged on accuracy, monotonicity and the spread between the first and last buckets.

requirements.statement: A double lift chart sorts observations by the ratio of one model's prediction to another model's prediction, groups them, and plots each model's average prediction and the actual value (normalized to the base) per group; the model whose line is closer to actual is better.

places.quote: A **double lift chart** compares two candidate models directly by sorting the data on the *ratio* of their predictions and plotting each model's average prediction against the actual over that sort.
Sorting on the ratio and grouping into equal-exposure quantiles $q$ isolates the risks on which the two **disagree most**; this is the [[Double Lift Chart|double lift chart]].

requirements.statement: Drawbacks of validation plots: quintile plots need separate plots per model and may be skewed by uneven risk sizes; double lift charts are hard to interpret and do not show actual dollar levels; loss ratio plots show only differentiation/ranking, not prediction accuracy.
Loss ratios used in validation must use on-level earned premium when rate changes have been implemented; otherwise the loss ratio plot can be misleading.

places.quote: **On-Level Premium** is historical earned premium restated as though every policy had been written at the rate level currently in effect.

**Calendar year** earned premium blends policy cohorts: CY 2024 earned premium comes from policies written in both $2023$ and $2024$, at whatever rates were then in force. That is why it must be brought to current level ([[On-Leveling]]) before use.

requirements.statement: For a negative binomial distribution with parameters r and p (in the form where the mean is rp/(1-p)), the mean equals rp/(1-p), which is solved for p given the mean and r.
For a negative binomial with parameters r and p, the probability of zero claims is Pr(N=0) = (1-p)^r.

places.quote: A zero-truncated distribution has $p_0^T = 0$ and $p_k^T = p_k/(1 - p_0)$.

requirements.statement: The experience modification factor for a group is Mod = Z × R + (1 − Z), where Z is the credibility of the group and R is the group's expected experience relative to the book average.

places.quote: $$M = Z \times \frac{A}{E} + (1 - Z)$$
$$M = Z\,\frac{A}{E} + (1 - Z) = \frac{A + K}{E + K}$$

requirements.statement: Credibility of experience rating depends not only on the volume of data (claims, exposures) but also on the variation in individual risk hazards within the class; greater heterogeneity of risks within a class gives experience rating more credibility.

places.quote: Credibility rises when risks genuinely differ from one another (large VHM) and falls when individual results are noisy (large EPV).
No class is perfectly [[Homogeneity|homogeneous]]: experience rating picks up the variance of the hypothetical means *within* a class.

requirements.statement: Experience rating is meant to distinguish individual risks within a class, so in a homogeneous or well-defined class with little variation in hazards, experience is less informative and receives lower credibility even if the class has high volume.

places.quote: because the mod measures only how far the record shows the risk to differ from others in its [[Rating Class|class]].
Bailey and Simon found that the more refined the class plan, the less credibility individual experience deserves.
Bailey and Simon showed that the more refined the classes, the less credibility individual experience deserves.

requirements.statement: The logit link, g(μ)=ln(μ/(1−μ)), is appropriate for a GLM with a binary target because its inverse, the logistic function, maps any linear predictor value in (−∞, ∞) to a value between 0 and 1 that can be interpreted as a probability.

places.quote: the **logit** [[Link Function]] maps the probability $\pi \in (0,1)$ onto the whole real line, so the linear predictor can take any value and the fitted probability always stays between $0$ and $1$.

requirements.statement: In a classification model, an observation is predicted positive when its modeled probability exceeds the discrimination threshold, converting a probability into a binary Yes/No prediction.

places.quote: A [[Logistic Regression|logistic]] or [[Classification Tree|tree]] model gives a probability; a **threshold** turns it into a decision.

requirements.statement: A confusion matrix tabulates actual versus predicted outcomes, giving true positives, false negatives, false positives, and true negatives.

places.quote: A **confusion matrix** cross-tabulates predicted class against actual class for a classifier, and is the table every classification metric is computed from.

requirements.statement: Sensitivity (true positive rate) = true positives / (true positives + false negatives), the proportion of actual positives predicted positive.

places.quote: \text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}
| **Sensitivity** (recall, TPR) | $\dfrac{TP}{TP + FN}$ | of the actual positives, how many were caught |

requirements.statement: Specificity (true negative rate) = true negatives / (true negatives + false positives); the false positive rate equals 1 − specificity.

places.quote: \text{FPR} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}
| **Specificity** (TNR) | $\dfrac{TN}{TN + FP}$ | of the actual negatives, how many were left alone |

places.quote: **ROC Curve**: plot of **True Positive Rate (Sensitivity)** vs. **False Positive Rate (1 − Specificity)** as the threshold varies.

requirements.statement: A model with no predictive power has an ROC curve along the 45-degree diagonal from (0,0) to (1,1), while a perfect model's ROC curve rises to (0,1) and then runs across to (1,1).

places.quote: No predictive power: the ROC curve follows the line of equality | | 1.0 | A perfect model: the ROC curve rises straight to the top of the graph

requirements.statement: When claims are more severe, the threshold should be lowered, since the cost of missing a fraudulent claim outweighs the cost of investigating extra claims; this raises sensitivity at the expense of more false positives.

places.quote: The two errors rarely cost the same: a missed fraud and a wrongly investigated honest claim have different price tags, and the threshold should reflect that rather than defaulting to 0.5
Lowering the threshold catches more true positives at the cost of more false positives.

requirements.statement: With a log link, the GLM predicted value is the exponential of the linear predictor (intercept plus coefficients times variable values), so each coefficient acts multiplicatively on the prediction.

places.quote: The **log link makes the model multiplicative**, so $e^{\beta}$ is a relativity and the fitted coefficients drop straight into a multiplicative [[Rating Algorithm|rating algorithm]].

The **log link** is standard for insurance severity and frequency models because it guarantees positive fitted values and allows multiplicative interpretation: a unit increase in $x_j$ multiplies $\mu$ by $e^{\beta_j}$

requirements.statement: To compute a fitted value, include a categorical level's coefficient only when the level applies (base level contributes zero), and include an interaction term's coefficient times its variable only when the interaction indicator applies.

A [[Categorical Predictor|categorical predictor]] with $k$ levels contributes $k - 1$ indicator columns (the omitted level is the base, absorbed into the intercept); an [[Interaction]] contributes the product of its columns; a quadratic term contributes a column of $x^2$

requirements.statement: The relativity between two risks under a log-link GLM is the exponential of the difference in their linear predictors, so terms common to both risks cancel in the ratio.

requirements.statement: To center a continuous predictor at its base level, add the predictor's main-effect coefficient times the base value (here ln of base AOI) to the original intercept; the main-effect and interaction coefficients are unchanged and the interaction is not included in the adjustment.
After centering at base levels, the intercept represents the predicted value (base rate) for a risk at all base levels, making it directly interpretable.

Centering makes coefficients of variables involved in interactions more intuitive, avoiding counterintuitive signs (e.g., a positive sprinklered coefficient) that arise when the continuous variable is zero outside the data's range; it does not change the continuous variable's own coefficient or significance, nor the number of parameters.
For a shifted Pareto severity with parameters alpha and beta, the mean is beta/(alpha-1) and the limited expected value at x is beta/(alpha-1) * [1 - (beta/(x+beta))^(alpha-1)].

places.quote: Losses are **capped** at a per-claim limit before entering $A$.
It is capped per claim, or split into primary and excess.

\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Premium}}

places.quote: The **Table M charge** $\phi(r) = \mathrm{E}[\max(A/E - r,\,0)]$ is the expected loss above $rE$ per unit of $E$
is Clark's **excess charge factor**, the share of expected aggregate loss above $A$.

$$E[S_{(a,\,b]}] = E[N]\,\big(E[X \wedge b] - E[X \wedge a]\big)$$

places.quote: applied to loss plus ALAE that has been adjusted for extraordinary events, development and trend.

requirements.statement: Premium = expected loss and LAE / (1 − variable expense ratio − risk load − profit load), with expense and profit loads taken as percentages of premium.

requirements.statement: The expected value of process variance (EVPV) is the average, across risks in a class, of the variance of each risk's own loss outcomes, measuring the randomness/volatility of an individual risk's experience.

places.quote: The **expected value of the process variance (EPV)**, written $v$, is the average within-risk variance in a [[Bühlmann Credibility]] model — how noisy a single risk's own experience is, averaged over the population of risks.
| $v = E[\sigma^2(\theta)]$ | Expected process variance | Expected within-risk variance |

requirements.statement: The variance of hypothetical means (VHM) is the variance across risks of each risk's expected loss, measuring how much the true risk levels differ from one another within a class (heterogeneity).

places.quote: The **variance of the hypothetical means (VHM)**, written $a$, is the between-risk variance in a [[Bühlmann Credibility]] model — how much the risks in the portfolio genuinely differ from one another once process noise is stripped out.
| $a = \text{Var}(\mu(\theta))$ | Variance of hypothetical means | Between-risk variance |

requirements.statement: Buhlmann credibility is Z = n/(n+k), where k = EVPV/VHM.

places.quote: - Together with the [[Variance of Hypothetical Means]] $a$ it fixes the Bühlmann constant $k = v/a$ and hence $Z = n/(n+k)$
- $K = \text{EPV}/\text{VHM}$ — expected value of the process variance over the variance of the hypothetical means.

requirements.statement: A higher VHM raises credibility (lower k) and a higher EVPV lowers credibility (higher k), so experience is more credible when risks differ greatly and individual experience is stable.

places.quote: - **Large $a$** means the risks are genuinely heterogeneous, so a risk's own experience is worth a lot and $Z$ rises
